variants.title: Run the evidence lifecycle
variants.context: An evaluation platform preserves a chain from a product claim to a reproducible measurement and an accountable decision. Version the claim and cases, execute a frozen configuration, combine independent judgments, then decide and learn.
variants.prompt: A team has a dashboard of scores but cannot explain last week's regression. Put the lifecycle stages in order.

items.text: Replay the application, retrieval, tools, prompts, and models with bounded concurrency and captured failures.
Attach deterministic checks, calibrated judges, human annotations, and adjudication to each case.
Apply the hard gates, preserve the decision record, and promote validated incidents into future datasets.
Record the behavior, risk slice, dataset snapshot, rubric, owner, and threshold before candidate results exist.

variants.hint: Thresholds declared after seeing the score are not thresholds.
variants.explanation: The platform's job is the chain from claim to measurement to decision, not the chart at the end of it.

variants.title: Run the evidence lifecycle
variants.context: An evaluation platform preserves a chain from a product claim to a reproducible measurement and an accountable decision. Version the claim and cases, execute a frozen configuration, combine independent judgments, then decide and learn.
variants.prompt: An engineer wants to rerun a six-week-old experiment to explain why a score moved. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Compare the two decision records and state which identity changed between them.
Replay the recorded application revision, prompts, tools, and retrieval index rather than the current ones.
Reapply the same code scorers, judge version, and stored human annotations to the replayed outputs.
Resolve the dataset snapshot, rubric version, risk labels, and threshold that the original run declared.

variants.hint: Reproduction means replaying the recorded configuration, not the current one.
variants.explanation: A score without its dataset, prompt, model, tools, and evaluator cannot explain a regression or support a release.

variants.title: Run the evidence lifecycle
variants.context: An evaluation platform preserves a chain from a product claim to a reproducible measurement and an accountable decision. Version the claim and cases, execute a frozen configuration, combine independent judgments, then decide and learn.
variants.prompt: A production incident produced twelve confirmed failures that the suite never covered. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Score them with the deterministic checker first, then route the disputed cases to human adjudication.
Record the decision and keep an untouched release holdout so the new cases cannot be tuned against.
Run the current application revision against that version with failures captured rather than retried silently.
Add the failures as a new dataset version with risk labels, an owner, and a declared floor.

variants.hint: New cases still need an owner and a threshold before they can gate anything.
variants.explanation: Validated incidents become a new dataset version, which is what keeps the suite current without erasing history.

variants.title: Fail closed on the evidence
variants.context: The lineage gate fails closed. Required artifacts must resolve to immutable versions, aggregate limits and critical-slice floors are applied separately, subjective decisions need calibrated agreement, and stale evidence expires.
variants.prompt: A release request arrives with a strong aggregate score and a missing reviewer decision ID. Put the gate checks in order.

items.text: Require calibrated agreement or adjudication wherever the decision rests on subjective judgment.
Expire the evidence if users, policies, documents, tools, or providers have materially changed since the run.
Treat a full pass as permission for a monitored canary rather than proof that global rollout is safe.
Apply the aggregate regression limit and each critical-slice floor as separate checks.
Confirm every required artifact exists and resolves to an immutable version, which this request fails.

variants.hint: A missing identity is a failure, not a warning to note beside a good score.
variants.explanation: The gate fails closed on missing evidence, so an unresolvable artifact blocks regardless of the aggregate.

variants.title: Fail closed on the evidence
variants.context: The lineage gate fails closed. Required artifacts must resolve to immutable versions, aggregate limits and critical-slice floors are applied separately, subjective decisions need calibrated agreement, and stale evidence expires.
variants.prompt: A candidate improves the average by 3.2 points while a safety slice sits at 78 percent against a 90 percent floor. Put the checks in order.

items.text: Read the aggregate limit and the safety floor as two separate checks, not one blended score.
Check that the evidence is recent enough to still describe the current policy and documents.
Confirm the safety judgments were calibrated or adjudicated before they are used to block.
Verify the dataset version, application revision, evaluator version, and decision ID all resolve.
Block the release on the failed floor instead of granting the canary the aggregate would allow.

variants.hint: Which check has a floor the average is not permitted to cross?
variants.explanation: Aggregate regression limits and hard floors for release-critical slices are applied separately, by design.

variants.title: Fail closed on the evidence
variants.context: The lineage gate fails closed. Required artifacts must resolve to immutable versions, aggregate limits and critical-slice floors are applied separately, subjective decisions need calibrated agreement, and stale evidence expires.
variants.prompt: Every artifact resolves and every threshold passes, but the run is 23 days old and the retrieval corpus was replaced last week. Put the checks in order.

items.text: Confirm reviewer agreement met its floor on the subjective dimensions.
Confirm the artifacts still resolve to the immutable versions the run recorded.
Apply the aggregate and critical-slice checks, both of which this candidate passes.
Expire the evidence, because the corpus change is a material change since the run.
Require a fresh run before any canary, since a passing but stale result is not current permission.

variants.hint: Passing thresholds and current evidence are two different conditions.
variants.explanation: Evidence expires after material changes to users, policies, documents, tools, or providers, however good the score was.

variants.title: Read capacity from the bottleneck
variants.context: Capacity is read from the bottleneck. Daily cases are cases per release times release attempts, review load is review cases against reviewer capacity, and runner hours are daily case seconds spread across the concurrency.
variants.prompt: Four trained reviewers each work 5 review hours per day and spend 6 minutes per case. How many cases can the review queue clear per day?
variants.hint: Reviewer hours and minutes per case are in different units.
variants.explanation: Review capacity is reviewers times review hours times sixty, divided by minutes per case. It is a hard ceiling that runner concurrency cannot raise.

mistakes.feedback: You multiplied by minutes per case instead of dividing by it.
You forgot to convert the review hours into minutes.

variants.title: Read capacity from the bottleneck
variants.context: Capacity is read from the bottleneck. Daily cases are cases per release times release attempts, review load is review cases against reviewer capacity, and runner hours are daily case seconds spread across the concurrency.
variants.prompt: A pipeline sends 270 cases per day to human review, and the reviewers can finish 200 cases per day. What is the review load in percent?
variants.hint: Load compares demand against the ceiling, in that order.
variants.explanation: A load above one hundred percent means the queue grows every day, so release decisions go stale even while automated scores finish quickly.

mistakes.feedback: You divided capacity by demand; load is demand against capacity.
You subtracted capacity from demand instead of dividing.

variants.title: Read capacity from the bottleneck
variants.context: Capacity is read from the bottleneck. Daily cases are cases per release times release attempts, review load is review cases against reviewer capacity, and runner hours are daily case seconds spread across the concurrency.
variants.prompt: A suite runs 4,800 cases per day at 6 seconds per case, with a runner concurrency of 40. How many hours of wall time does the run take?
variants.hint: Concurrency divides the total work before it is converted into hours.
variants.explanation: Runner hours are daily cases times seconds per case, divided by concurrency and then by 3600. Adding concurrency helps only until provider limits dominate.

mistakes.feedback: You forgot to divide by the runner concurrency.
That is the wall time in seconds, not hours.

variants.title: Choose the operating model
variants.context: Operating models differ in what they own. Managed services reduce integration work, self-hostable platforms give data locality and deployment control, an existing experiment ecosystem consolidates tooling, and a hybrid control plane keeps canonical evidence portable.
variants.prompt: A regulated insurer must keep evaluation traces inside one region and control the storage that holds them.
options: An open or self-hostable platform, with upgrades and incident ownership costed in.
A framework-integrated managed service, since traces already flow through that framework.
A managed evaluation-first service, with a contractual commitment on regional storage.
optionFeedback: Self-hosting gives data locality and storage control at the cost of owning upgrades, backups, and incidents.
Low integration friction does not address the requirement that the data stay in owned infrastructure.
A contract about a region still leaves the storage outside the team's own control.
variants.hint: Which requirement is about where the bytes live rather than how convenient the workflow is?
variants.explanation: Start from data boundaries and failure ownership, then verify current documentation with a representative pilot.

variants.title: Choose the operating model
variants.context: Operating models differ in what they own. Managed services reduce integration work, self-hostable platforms give data locality and deployment control, an existing experiment ecosystem consolidates tooling, and a hybrid control plane keeps canonical evidence portable.
variants.prompt: A team already runs model experiments, artifacts, and access control in one platform, and now wants LLM evaluation beside them.
options: Build a composable internal platform so every contract can be defined from scratch.
Adopt a second managed service and keep the two tool sets synchronized by export.
Adopt the existing experiment ecosystem, then verify its review and release workflows.
optionFeedback: Owning every contract is justified by regulation or unique scale, neither of which is present here.
Two sources of truth create a synchronization burden without answering any product requirement.
Consolidated tooling reuses existing identity and access, and the open question is review and release depth.
variants.hint: What does this team already own that a new tool would duplicate?
variants.explanation: Consolidation is a real operating model, but it still has to be pilot-tested for release and review workflows.

variants.title: Choose the operating model
variants.context: Operating models differ in what they own. Managed services reduce integration work, self-hostable platforms give data locality and deployment control, an existing experiment ecosystem consolidates tooling, and a hybrid control plane keeps canonical evidence portable.
variants.prompt: A team wants managed runners and annotation tooling, but is unwilling to let its datasets and release policy become unportable.
options: Accept the managed platform as the system of record and rely on its export feature later.
Self-host everything so that no vendor ever holds any part of the evaluation workflow.
Keep canonical datasets, manifests, and policy in owned storage while using managed runners.
optionFeedback: Deferring the export question is how migration cost becomes discovered rather than chosen.
Self-hosting the whole stack solves portability by taking on operations the team did not ask for.
A hybrid control plane keeps the evidence portable while renting execution and review tooling.
variants.hint: Which pieces must the team still own for a migration to stay cheap?
variants.explanation: The hybrid control plane reduces migration risk but adds integration and identity boundaries that need testing.

variants.title: Sort the five identities
variants.context: A platform result carries five identities: test identity is the cases, application identity is the system under test, execution identity is the run itself, judgment identity is the scoring, and decision identity is the release action.
variants.prompt: A platform result lists five groups of fields. Match each group to the identity it records.

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: Dataset version, split, case ID, provenance, and risk labels.

pairs.label: Application identity
pairs.detail: Source revision, prompt, model, tools, retrieval index, and runtime image.

pairs.label: Execution identity
pairs.detail: Run ID, timestamps, retries, provider errors, latency, and raw output.

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: Code scorer, judge model and prompt, rubric, reviewer, and adjudication version.

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: Baseline, thresholds, approver, rollout scope, abort signal, and rollback owner.

variants.hint: Two of these describe the system under test and the act of running it, which are not the same thing.
variants.explanation: Separating execution from application identity is what lets a provider error be told apart from a behavior change.

variants.title: Sort the five identities
variants.context: A platform result carries five identities: test identity is the cases, application identity is the system under test, execution identity is the run itself, judgment identity is the scoring, and decision identity is the release action.
variants.prompt: Five details are missing from a disputed experiment. Match each missing detail to its identity.

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: The sampling policy that chose which cases entered the run.

pairs.label: Application identity
pairs.detail: The tool versions the application called during the replay.

pairs.label: Execution identity
pairs.detail: The number of retries the runner performed after provider timeouts.

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: The reviewer who resolved the disagreements on this batch.

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: The exception that was approved and the date it expires.

variants.hint: Retries belong to the act of running, not to the system being run.
variants.explanation: A failed model call, a failed scorer, and a low score are different states, and only stored identities keep them apart.

variants.title: Sort the five identities
variants.context: A platform result carries five identities: test identity is the cases, application identity is the system under test, execution identity is the run itself, judgment identity is the scoring, and decision identity is the release action.
variants.prompt: A review meeting asks five questions about one experiment. Match each question to the identity that answers it.

pairs.label: Test identity
pairs.detail: Which risk labels were attached to the cases that failed?

pairs.label: Application identity
pairs.detail: Which retrieval index did these answers read from?

pairs.label: Execution identity
pairs.detail: How many cases never completed because the provider returned an error?

pairs.label: Judgment identity
pairs.detail: Which rubric version decided that these answers passed?

pairs.label: Decision identity
pairs.detail: What rollout scope did this result authorize, and who signed it?

variants.hint: One of these questions is about what did not finish rather than what scored badly.
variants.explanation: If a result can be published without immutable inputs, evaluator identity, and a decision record, the tool tracks experiments but does not govern evidence.
